Trump dominating media attention with unfiltered daily press briefings

They've become a nightly ritual for millions of Americans who are stuck at home. Around the time most local TV stations typically air the nightly news, President Donald Trump and members of the White House coronavirus task force break in for an update on the coronavirus pandemic.

It's the very definition of must-see television. Americans are tuned in, many are worried and looking for answers at a time of widespread uncertainty, regardless of whether they like the president or hate him.

According to polling by the Trump campaign, 84% of likely voters watch all part of the president's daily briefings.

Politically, they appear to have buoyed Trump, at least temporarily. A Gallup Poll from the end of March found that 60% of Americans approved of Trump's handling of the pandemic. A Morning Consult survey released Monday suggested that the support declined over the past week to 49%.

Trump's overall job approval is up to 47%, up more than 5% over recent months.

“Americans want to see their president out front and leading in a time of crisis and that’s exactly what President Trump is doing," said Tim Murtaugh, the Trump campaign communications director. "He is keeping people informed about what their government is doing to protect their safety and safeguard the economy."

Some critics have questioned the polls as well as Trump's leadership in the face of the pandemic, but the bump in approval matches the country's historic response.

"In times of crisis, and the current pandemic is arguably the most serious crisis faced by anyone under 75, Americans tend to rally behind their president," said Mark Jones, a political science professor at Rice University's Baker Institute.

Trump's crisis approval ratings are far short of President George W. Bush's 90% approval ratings after the Sept. 11, 2001, or Franklin Roosevelt's 84% approval after the attack on Pearl Harbor.

The pandemic has provided Trump with an opportunity to be less divisive and more presidential, "to bring Americans together with the common goal of defeating the COVID-19 virus rather than dividing them for the purpose of electoral victory," Jones said.

It's an open question of how Trump will use that opportunity.

INFORMATION SESSIONS OR TRUMP RALLIES?

On most nights, cable news networks CNN, Fox News and MSNBC have carried the briefings that last anywhere from one to nearly two-and-a-half hours. MSNBC has stopped broadcasting it in full and the other networks have interrupted the briefings.

The extent of the unfiltered coverage of the president has caused an outcry in some quarters.

In a tirade last week, MSNBC anchor Chris Hayes argued that the daily briefings have "morphed into something akin to Trump rallies without the crowds."

He was not alone in the observation. A MoveOn.org petition with nearly 300,000 signatures called on CNN, ABC, CBS, NBC, NPR and Fox News to stop broadcasting full live coverage of the news conferences, arguing the president is "blatantly using the news organizations’ extensive, live coverage to freely campaign for a second term."

MoveOn.org petition calling on networks to stop airing President Trump's daily coronavirus briefings. (MoveOn.org)

The petition further warned that it was "wrong and dangerous to provide so much unfettered airtime" to the president who has regularly made false or misleading statements about the pandemic.

Republican strategist Ford O'Connell dismissed the criticism as "disingenuous," noting, "Anyone who says these are Trump rallies has obviously never been to a Trump rally."

The televised appearances are clearly beneficial to the president's reelection campaign, O'Connell continued. They feature combative interactions with reporters, which have consistently appealed to his base. That Trump continues to hold them on a daily basis demonstrates that he thinks they're helping him.

"What I really hear people saying is, he's getting too much television time to dominate the narrative," O'Connell said. "You have to recognize, people are scared. They're worried about the future and their livelihood and frankly, they want to get information straight from Trump's mouth, or at least from the White House task force."

The MoveOn petition was just one of several calls for news outlets to stop broadcasting the president's briefings.

MSNBC anchor Rachel Maddow argued that if it were up to her, she would "stop putting those briefings on live TV. Not out of spite, but because it’s misinformation."

CNN anchor Don Lemon questioned whether his network should carry live coverage of the president, saying "Those press briefings have become his new 'Apprentice.'"

Vox.com co-founder Matthew Yglesias called on cable news networks to "cancel the Trump Show." Arguing that Trump has a right to address the nation about the crisis, he claimed that "no president in American history has ever had the privilege of having his every word simulcast across news networks."

Only a short time ago, there were complaints about the White House holding too few press briefings. Some critics are now faulting the White House for too extensive briefings.

As one opinion writer suggested, it's reminiscent of the joke about the patron complaining about the restaurant where the food was awful and the portions were too small.

SUCKING UP 'ALL THE OXYGEN'

The presidential election is less than seven months away and like the 2016 election, Trump is dominating the news cycle.

"When Trump was campaigning four years ago people would talk about how he sucked up all the oxygen, that all the attention is on him," said Mitchell McKinney director of the University of Missouri Political Communication Institute.

In a typical evening, the press briefing will last one to two hours, followed by news networks fact-checking, replaying clips or otherwise commenting on the president's remarks or news from the task force.
